etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τεχνολογία (tekhnología, “systematic treatment (of grammar)”), from τέχνη (tékhnē, “art”) + -λογία (-logía, “study”). By surface analysis, techno- +‎ -logy.

definitions.definition: The combined application of science and art in practical ways in industry, as for example in designing new machines.

quote.citation: 2013 June 21, Chico Harlan, “Japan pockets the subsidy …”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 2, page 30:
quote.text: Across Japan, technology companies and private investors are racing to install devices that until recently they had little interest in: solar panels. Massive solar parks are popping up as part of a rapid build-up that one developer likened to an "explosion."

definitions.definition: (countable) Any useful skill or mechanism that humans have developed or invented (including in prescientific eras).
(countable, figurative) Any useful trait that has evolved in any organism.

quote.citation: 2012, Caspar Henderson, The Book of Barely Imagined Beings, page 317:
quote.text: Comb jellies lack the most impressive 'technology' of jellyfish - the nematocyst stinging apparatus which is one of the most deadly weapons and fastest cellular processes in nature.

definitions.definition: (uncountable, academic) The study of or a collection of techniques.
(archaic) A discourse or treatise on the arts.
